title: When You Shouldn't Enforce A Consequence https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/11/18/when-you-shouldnt-enforce-a-consequence/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin identifies a narrow but important exception to the rule of always enforcing consequences: when a well-behaved student breaks a minor rule, such as calling out, specifically to stop a classmate from interfering with their right to learn. He argues that holding this student strictly accountable would alienate a role model who has bought into the classroom culture, sending the wrong message about fairness and favoritism. Instead, he recommends preventing the situation altogether through vigilant supervision, and if it does happen, quietly apologizing to the student afterward rather than publicly explaining the decision to the class. Linsin frames this as an example of respecting the spirit of a rule over its letter, which paradoxically strengthens rather than undermines a teacher's consistency. The piece closes by connecting this compassionate judgment call to greater trust, relatability, and authority in the classroom.
points: There is a narrow exception to strict consequence enforcement: when a student breaks a rule in order to protect their own right to learn from a disruptive classmate.
The best solution is preventive — vigilant observation and supervision so the triggering misbehavior is caught before a good student feels the need to speak up.
If the situation is missed, the teacher should still hold only the original disruptor accountable, not the student who reacted.
A private, later apology to the student who spoke up reassures them that protecting the class is the teacher's job, not theirs.
Showing this kind of judgment makes a teacher appear more human and trustworthy, not inconsistent or unfair.
quotes: One of the core tenets of SCM is to hold your students accountable for every rule violation. You do what you say you’re going to do. You follow through on your promises.
It’s when a student calls out without permission in order to stop a classmate from interfering with their right to learn.
Now, if you were to follow your classroom management plan as written and hold this student accountable for calling out, you would very likely alienate them.
Bear in mind that this is a student who has fully bought into the culture of your classroom. They care about learning and represent what you’re trying to inspire in others.
However, it’s important that you don’t just leave it at that. When you get a chance, later in the day, briefly apologize to the student who felt they had to stand up for themselves.
You’re showing understanding and compassion, and at the same time, making a statement through your actions that you respect the difference between the literal rule and the true spirit of the rule.
It makes you more human, more like them. It proves that you’re not a dictator, a robot, or a narrow-minded stickler without common sense.
